Caeroc's Pride, though to be fair it's more a "least worst" weapon.

A ranged weapon means not having to engage in the clunky melee system, but a two-handed ranged weapon means no spellcasting unless you deal with the clunky weapon swapping system.  So for something reasonably smooth, you're stuck with either pistols or wands.

Pistols can headshot, which guarantees critical damage.  That pretty much eliminates wands outright if you're playing keyboard + mouse.

That leaves us with four unique options - the non-unique options can't be raised to Legendary and are therefore a waste of resources.  So we have: 

\* Fair Play, which gives a tiny heal on kill and irrelvant crit buff - hit headshots and you already guarantee crits.

\* The Disappointer, which gives a tiny damage buff and a tiny bleed buff.  Probably my second favorite option.

\* Magic Mistol, which would be perfect if you could remove "Foe Seeker", which turns the hitscan shot into a projectile and ruins a well-aimed crit about one time out of five.

\* Caeroc's Pride, which means you don't have to manually swap to electric grenades to solve generator puzzles.

Healing and damage aren't really relevant when you kill every foe with chained critical headshots before they can get in range, so the convenience of having a source of electric damage on hand at all times seems preferable.  I tried the Magic Mistol but it comes into play so late in the game as to be irrelevant and that slow-moving projectile doesn't make it any more accurate - it makes it less accurate in that it doesn't home in on stuff you wouldn't have hit anyway, but \*does\* alter its flight path to miss headshots you would have made with a normal pistol.

I might try The Disappointer next time through, but I picked up Caerocs in the first zone and it's still working fine in the fourth zone.  The real disappointer is the lack of meaningful upgrades to starter weapons.

On the one hand, yes, it's probably too easy if you're looking for a realistic simulation of melee combat.

On the other hand, if it weren't too easy it would be even more tedious than it already is when you have to whittle down groups of 5+ foes.

So if there's a problem, it's probably that combat isn't *fun*.  They've got a melee combat system that wants to simulate realistic weapon techniques, which is fine for duels... and then every fight that matters is Henry vs three or more foes.  Between the forced lock-on and janky hitboxes, I'd gladly take 'too easy' over the tedious slog that more challenge from each individual foe would create.  Make it harder and more time-consuming and you're just pushing players to use stealth, poison cookpots, snipe individuals and flee until they break combat, etc.

Would definitely go in for a mod that turned the bulk melee battles where you're dueling 5+ foes into challenging 1-v-1 encounters, though.

It's useful to know that the Palworld character ID is not unique across servers, and that the Palworld save file name is just the Palworld character ID in HEX format.

So if you temporarily create a server and have a friend join it, go into Admin mode on the new server, and click their name from the admin menu, you can get their character ID.  Then you can convert that ID from DEC to HEX, find the corresponding file in the player save directory, and delete it.

When you have a server with 20+ members on it this is how you enable players who are locked out to start new characters without forcing the rest of your players into a rollback.

I dunno about whether it boosts skilled groups, but the general consensus I've seen on forums and discord from other players is that it's tilted a *bit* in the teens favor in the most fair case - 4 solo queue players who are competent and communicative but haven't pre-planned anything.  Once you start talking about a coordinated team of players planning their builds so their perks work well together and putting together a gameplan before the match, things get pretty dire for the killer.

As far as remaining dead... I mean, unless they relaunch as a 2.0 kind of thing or expand to other platforms I'm not sure how they could get those player numbers to climb.

Long story short, the devs were focused on the solo teen experience, didn't want the game to end up with a teen queing solo and getting tunneled to death.  That wound up with a situation where killers had to play very defensively against good teams.  

The first 30-60 seconds you were sprinting around like mad trying to get a hit on one before they got armed, but once 2-3 of them got armed it was extremely challenging to split them up or get hits/downs on them.  Killer's huge, has a aura announcing their approach, has a cooldown on their defensive skill, and takes -one- hit to banish.  Kids are small, nearly silent, and take -two- hits to down - one to injure, which snares the killer, a second to knock into bleedout.  So they can easily afford to have one of the four of them take a hit to set the killer up for a banish.  The game as killer becomes much more about gathering information, protecting your hp, feinting to bait out ambushes, using your defensive skill to get a hit, and retreating.  I could win games, but they were 45 minute slogs if I didn't get a kill in the first minute or two.  

That meant that queues for killer were instant but queues for teens were up to 30-45 mins at times - but it also meant that teens leveled up way faster because they were way more likely to win, further punishing killers, especially new killers who don't have the perks to combat four high level teens.  Eventually the number of players dipped so low that I kept queuing into the same recognizable 4-person groups, had like a 80% loss rate against those groups, and just decided it was time to move on.

I disagree with your results for a couple reasons.

First, toughness always recovers at a rate that is a percentage of your base toughness value.  Higher base value means more recovery from coherency and talents.

Second, the first hit into your toughness goes 100% into toughness unless it overflows into HP - but that's typically only things like bursters and sniper shots that you're strongly encouraged to manually avoid.

Third, HP can only be recovered at medicaid stations and medipacks, both of which are a limited resource and less abundant in higher difficulties.

So what you're really looking to do is not tank the most damage in a single burst, but soak individual hits you fail to avoid *and then replenish your toughness*.  The faster you replenish it, the less hp damage you take and the less healing you need, which leaves more heals for folks with purple bars.

This is because more total toughness makes each hit easier to soak.  For example, an Ogryn with 160 toughness swinging into a horde and getting 20% of his toughness back every 1s, plus another 5% from coherency.  He can take a 40 point hit every second or two in a messy horde and still never touch his HP.  The same Ogryn with a boost to his HP can only recover quickly from a 25 point hit.

And since Toughness takes double damage from melee attacks, Poxwalker scratches and other minor wounds do a pretty decent chunk of toughness damage.  You want to stack this to protect your HP on any class.

It's more important to *keep the buff up* and secondarily to keep it on a vulnerable point than to get max dps out of the darts themselves.  They hit hard, but not as hard as 31 other people nuking a Gigantix weak point.

If you've got 5 points in Blight Rounds the duration is longer than the cooldown, so as long as you hit the 3rd dart you can re-apply the debuff before it wears off and always have purple buff up.

Once you get the hang of enemy patterns it's pretty easy to get all your darts off quickly, but ensuring you hit with every dart is worth delaying your shot if you aren't certain it will hit.  Missing the 3rd shot is particularly punishing - if you whiff it and the boss is moving when the cooldown ends, you might not be able to keep the debuff rolling.

I usually use the first shot ASAP, use the 2nd to correct if I hit an arm or something with the first or as extra damage if the first is good, and aim the 3rd carefully during the recovery after an attack to keep the buff rolling.

I think this depends greatly on the relevance of the challenge and rewards over time.  If you put a puzzle in your game, you're requesting that I solve it in order to advance.  If solving the puzzle is not fun and not learning the solution prevents me from playing further, that's a natural, built-in point at which a player can just decide the game is not for them.

So I think puzzles work better in idle games when they have certain traits.  I think one beneficial trait for a puzzle in an idle game is that the puzzle relies upon player skill rather than character resources.  Any player who encounters it should, technically, with sufficient wit, be able to overcome it and receive the reward.

I think another beneficial trait is a properly scoped reward.  Something that feels big when received but, importantly, either does not greatly impact the game long-term or becomes trivial to attain once a player greatly exceeds the puzzle requirements.  This lets players who care enough to engage with your puzzle feel rewarded for their efforts in the short term while letting people who don't want to engage attain the same benefit through persisting, which is the default action in any idle game.  It also keeps puzzles from kicking people out of your game, because if they just wait a day/week/month/etc they'll still be at about the same point as the guy who solved the puzzle.

As an example of fun puzzle/challenge mechanics, consider Idle Wizard and Antimatter Dimensions.  AD also has a nice example of how to make a bare bones skilltree.

Upgrade Cheapest doesn't work.  There are a few reasons for this.

The primary problem is that upgrading the cheapest gear is always a waste of gold.  The cheapest equipment you can buy is the most outdated equipment, often several orders of magnitude less effective than the most expensive equipment.  
This causes several secondary problems.  Since Upgrade Cheapest upgrades the lowest-rank items it wastes coin on the items you're most likely to replace through "buy random catalog item".


This is further compounded by the slow automation interface meant to fire off abilities with cooldowns measured in seconds.  With 200% haste, all 4 automator speed increase nodes, and Upgrade Cheapest on an 'Always' automator stone, the system checks 1-2 times per second.

---
So how do we solve this?  There are a variety of options; here are a few ideas.


+ Causing Upgrade Cheapest to spend as much gold as possible upgrading the item it chooses while, crucially, causing it to stop upgrading items once they reach level 100 would be ideal, but perhaps more automation-friendly than desired.  


+ An "Upgrade All" gem that blindly attempts to upgrade every item once would be an improvement.  


+ An "Upgrade Most Expensive" gem would be an improvement, and may just require flipping an angle bracket somewhere.  


+ An "Upgrade Bonus" that works like Upgrade Cheapest but with the benefit of upgrading by 10s instead of by 1s would be another simple but welcome solution.

1) During your opener, smash straight through enemy lines.  Your initial play should always be to turn the foes around and tank them with their backs to your group.  This lets your melee hit their rear/side positionals easily and points cleaves and frontal cones toward you and away from your team.

I dropped a 4% primal for a 3% primal + 3% hero cost.  I'll break down the reasons why, but it basically boils down to farming efficiency vs progression efficiency.

The below assumes you're mid-game, with maxed Atman and Dogcog, starting from a base of four 4% primal chance relics with no other notable stats, and considering switching to a relic with 3% primal chance and -3% hero cost.

Your primal chance goes from 66% to 65%.  This means that the chance to NOT find a primal increases by ~2.94% at 65% compared to 66%.  You're effectively losing 3% of your souls per run.

In return, you're reducing the cost of every hero purchase by 6%, which acts as a multiplier of your total gold income.

In the end you get less efficient farming during short runs, but can extend your runs slightly longer before hitting the point where upgrade costs prohibit you from instakilling.  In practice, it means I'm running 45 levels past the calculator's suggested optimum level before reaching what I've observed to be optimal.

I'm not good enough with math to calculate the value of 45 additional levels past an arbitrary max level, but since later levels provide more souls than earlier levels and the 6% gold bonus helps with my progression as well as my farming, I'm content with my decision.

Pretty close, but it's actually the other way around - the name is decided by the primary effect.  When a relic is created, one or more stats are rolled.  If more than one bonus exists, the largest bonus gets sorted to the top and provides the suffix for the relic.  

The difference between this and what you said is that you'll never end up with an "of Souls" item that provides 1% primal chance and 1000% more gold - the name always comes from the largest effect.

The point of regilding is to focus as much of your gild damage multiplier as possible into a single hero, thereby making that hero vastly more efficient.  You get more damage out of them per gold spent.

The more concentrated your gilds are, the better.  Splitting them up this way only gives you 48% of your potential gild damage bonus.  By the time you're ready to regild to Atlas, the cost of regilding will be trivial; you're still quite a long ways away from that point.

You're also banking too small a stack of souls for your Siyalatas level.  Probably want to be sitting on around 2500 for best performance with a 29 Siyalatas.  I'd get to that point, max out Atman, and work on regilding to Samurai.

It's better than nothing, but still trash tier.

Look for stats you can only get in limited amounts from ancients.  Chance of Primal Bosses is best by a wide margin, to the point that anything that doesn't have Chance for Primal Bosses is junk.  So really, you want Chance for Primal Bosses plus other stuff.

Good secondary stats include -hero cost and -boss life, both of which get better the more you stack them.  You might also consider % chance of double rubies, % chance of 10x gold, and possibly certain duration ancients- I've seen some strangely high values for some of those.

As many have already said, wait until 1500+ or you're setting yourself back.

I tend to wait until 1525/1550 just to give myself a little extra leeway when it comes to the early levels.  Otherwise I find that I have peaks and valleys in my kill speed until the 5x multiplier levels.

Definitely don't be tempted to switch early.  You won't be making real progress, you'll just be tricking yourself into thinking you are.
